title: Course enrollment day
brief: Registration opens at 9 am for 40,000 students, and a handful of popular courses have only 30 seats each. Everyone clicks "enroll" at the same moment, and when the page is slow they click again. A seat must go to exactly one student.

clarify.q: How wrong can the seat count shown on the page be?
clarify.a: A few seconds late is fine. The final check happens when you press enroll.

clarify.q: Can a student enroll twice in the same course?
clarify.a: No. A repeated click or a retry must not count twice, and must not take two seats.
About twelve times normal traffic for fifteen minutes, with a third of all lookups going to the same few courses.
Yes. When a page fails they click again quickly, which makes things worse.

notes: A "write" is an enroll, a drop or a swap.
Seat counts shown on the page may be a little behind; the booking is exact.
Notification speed measures provider acceptance. Device receipt is outside this traffic model; check expiry, provider outcome and retries in the correctness trace before claiming delivery guarantees.

hints: A third of the traffic wants the same few rows. What keeps one row from being the whole database's problem?
Slow the retries at the door: a rate limiter per student stops the retry storm from feeding itself.
Releasing a seat needs the same atomic state discipline as claiming it. Measure the failed boundary, waiting time and retry work before choosing a change.

editorial.summary: Seats are a hot row. Reads of the course page can be copied; the seat grant cannot, so it is serialised through a queue. Rate limiting and an idempotency store turn the panic of retries into harmless noise.

designs.name: Copy the pages, queue the seats
designs.why: A CDN and a replica answer the course pages from copies. A per-student rate limiter flattens the clicking. Enroll requests ride a queue to workers that update the primary one at a time, and an idempotency store makes a repeated enroll a no-op.

tradeoffs: A strict queue grants seats in order and keeps the database calm, but each student waits a moment longer to hear "you got in".
A 5-second page copy can show "1 seat left" when it is gone; the queue decides, and the student sees a clear message.
A per-student limit of 3 per second never bothers a normal person and removes most of the retry storm.
Splitting a hot course into several counters is faster still, but complicates fairness; the queue is simpler to explain.
editorial.realWorld: University registration systems have long been known for crashing at the minute seats open; typical fixes are staggered start times by year, queues for the enroll step and aggressive caching of course lists (approx.).

correctness.prompt: Two students claim the last seat, and one retries. What constraint and transaction prevent overselling or enrolling a student twice?
correctness.discussion: Enforce a unique constraint on course and student. In one transaction, create the enrollment and decrement remaining capacity only when it is positive. Roll back both changes on conflict. A repeated request returns the existing enrollment. A queue can smooth demand, but concurrent consumers still need the constraint and atomic capacity check. The capacity condition must hold at commit, not at the earlier page read. An enrollment key prevents a retry consuming a second seat. Releasing a seat needs the same atomic state discipline as claiming it.

fields.label: Step 1. Two students read one remaining seat. What commits?
options: One enrollment and a conditional capacity decrement in one transaction
fields.explanation: The capacity condition must hold at commit, not at the earlier page read.

fields.label: Step 2. The winner retries after losing the response. What is returned?
options: The existing enrollment under course and student uniqueness
fields.explanation: An enrollment key prevents a retry consuming a second seat.

fields.label: Step 3. A cancellation races with a duplicate cancellation. How is capacity restored?
options: Transition enrolled to cancelled once and increment capacity in the same transaction
Increment capacity on every cancellation request
fields.explanation: Releasing a seat needs the same atomic state discipline as claiming it.

correctness.responsibility: Allocate the last course seat atomically and make enrollment retries safe.
correctness.limits: The traffic model does not execute this protocol. The checked trace covers its central responsibility; the written explanation is retained for review.

twist.brief: Demand has settled at about 400 requests/s. The new monthly ceiling is $12784. The original burst reserve now competes with the operating budget. Decide which reserve to keep, then test its failure headroom. All data and recovery promises still apply.

design.name: Smaller workload, measured reserve
design.why: Reduce the paid floor for the quieter workload, preserving the required copies and recovery settings. This design was checked through the full event day.
